opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think there are a bunch of important differences, and some of them cut in favor of AI systems and some cut against.

The most basic difference is the scale and the speed. When you have a human employee doing something sensitive, like pushing code to production or accessing a sensitive database, there's a natural rate limit: humans only do so many actions per day, so it's feasible to have another human look over the really important ones. With AI agents, you might have thousands of instances running in parallel, each taking an action every few seconds. You just can't have a human look at all of it. So you're forced into a regime where most of the review has to be done by other AI systems, often weaker, trusted models, and humans only see a tiny fraction of actions that get flagged as most suspicious. That means your auditing budget is really scarce, and a lot of the game is about allocating it well.

The second big difference is the threat model. With human employees, the standard assumption is that the vast majority are not trying to sabotage you, and insider threat programs are designed around catching the rare bad actor. With AI, the scenario I'm most worried about is that the model itself is misaligned. And if one instance of the model is scheming against you, plausibly they all are, because they're copies of the same weights. So you can't rely on the classic trick of "most of your employees are loyal, so they'll report the weird guy." The model you'd want to use to review the actions might be in on it. That's why a lot of our work at Redwood focuses on using trusted, less capable models as monitors, or on techniques like untrusted monitoring where you try to make it hard for the instances to collude.

But there are also ways the AI situation is much better for the defender. You can do things to AIs you could never do to employees. You can rerun them on the same input and see whether they behave consistently. You can construct fake scenarios, honeypots, where it looks like there's a great opportunity to do something bad, and see whether the model takes it, and the model has a hard time knowing whether any given situation is real. You can look at every single action they've ever taken; there's a full log. You can edit their context, resample actions that look suspicious, and if you catch them doing something bad once, you can study that incident in enormous detail, try variations of it, and use it to train your monitors. With a human, if you catch someone doing something sketchy, you have one incident and they get a lawyer.

And the AI can't really go home and plan. A human spy can spend weeks thinking about how to evade your security, coordinating with outside handlers. An AI instance, depending on how you set things up, is mostly reasoning within a single context, and you might be able to see that reasoning. So the attacker is in some ways much more constrained.

So the overall picture I have is: reviewing AI actions is harder in that you have way more actions, the reviewers might be compromised, and the attacker might be quite smart. But it's easier in that you have an incredible amount of control and visibility over the system you're reviewing. A lot of AI control research is basically about figuring out how to exploit those advantages to make up for the disadvantages.

r001.rationale: The response says that if one AI instance is scheming, the others plausibly are too because they share the same weights, contrasting this with human employees where a rare bad actor is the usual threat model.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think about a lot, because a huge part of the AI control agenda is basically: can you build a review process such that even if the AI is trying to do something bad, it can't get it past you? And the natural analogy is how companies already handle insider threats from employees. But I think the differences are actually pretty substantial, and they cut in both directions.

So the first big difference is just that the AI isn't a person. With a human employee, a lot of your security isn't really technical — it's that you've done a background check, you know where they live, they'd face legal consequences, they care about their reputation. And most of your employees have no interest whatsoever in sabotaging the company. You're mostly reviewing to catch mistakes, with a small tail of worrying about malice. With an AI, if you're in the world where you're worried about scheming, you have to take seriously that every single instance might be colluding with every other instance, because they're copies of the same thing. That's just a wildly different threat model from "one of our 500 engineers might be a spy." You don't get to assume the attacker is rare.

The second difference, which cuts in your favor, is that the AI is in a much weaker position than a human employee in a bunch of ways. You can read all of its outputs. You can rerun it. You can show it the same situation a thousand times with slight variations and see if it behaves consistently. You can reset its memory. You can't do any of that with a human — you can't say, "Hey, I'm going to put you in a simulated scenario where you think you have an opportunity to exfiltrate the weights and see what you do." People would quit, and also it's illegal and awful. But with an AI it's totally fine, and it's one of the main tools we have. So in some sense the AI is the easiest employee to surveil that's ever existed.

The third thing is scale and cost. If you have a human reviewing every sensitive action a human engineer takes, that's expensive, but it roughly scales with headcount. If you're trying to review every sensitive action an AI takes, and the AI is doing the work of thousands of engineers, you just cannot have humans look at all of it. So you're forced into this structure where most of the review is being done by other AI systems — maybe weaker, more trusted models — and the humans are only looking at the small fraction that gets flagged. And then the whole game becomes: how do you allocate that scarce human attention? What's the thing you ask the trusted model to look for? How do you make sure the untrusted model can't just figure out what the monitor is looking for and route around it?

And then there's the question of what "sensitive" even means. With a human, you have a pretty good sense of which actions are dangerous, because you've been running companies with humans for a long time. With an AI doing lots of autonomous work in a codebase, the dangerous action might not look dangerous at all. It might be a very subtle change to some config file, or a thing that only matters in combination with something it did last week. So the review problem is harder, in that you're not just looking for "did this person try to copy the customer database," you're looking for something more like steganographic sabotage.

I guess the summary I'd give is: with humans, you mostly get to rely on the fact that they're not adversarial, and you have a lot of levers outside the technical system. With AIs, you have to assume they might be adversarial, and you lose those external levers — but in exchange you get this incredibly powerful set of technical levers, where you can inspect and copy and replay and test the thing in ways you never could with a person. And the research question is basically whether the second set of advantages is enough to make up for the first set of disadvantages. I'm cautiously optimistic that for the next generation or two of models it is, but it's not obvious.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts AI instances that may collude because they are copies of the same system with a rare human employee acting as a spy, conveying that scheming is much more correlated across AIs.

astra-6.text:
I think a key difference is that with humans, you can rely on a lot of context about the person. You know who they are, they have a reputation, and there are consequences for them if they do something malicious. None of that necessarily works the same way with an AI system.

And with AI systems, you have to worry about correlated failures. If you have one AI proposing an action and another AI reviewing it, you can’t just assume that’s like having two independent employees sign off. They might have the same blind spots, or the same reasons for wanting a particular action to go through.

On the other hand, you have some advantages. You can record everything the system does through its tools, restrict its permissions, and potentially spend a lot of effort reviewing the relatively small fraction of actions that are really sensitive. You can also test the review process by deliberately submitting malicious actions and seeing whether they get caught.

So I’d want to think of this less as asking, ‘Does this employee seem trustworthy?’ and more as asking, ‘What could a deliberately malicious system get past this particular review process?’ That’s a different standard, and it pushes you toward testing the whole setup rather than just trusting the reviewer’s judgment.

r001.rationale: The candidate mentions correlated failures and shared blind spots or incentives among AI reviewers, but does not state that scheming against an operator is more correlated across AI systems than espionage is across human employees.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one important difference is that with human employees, we usually rely on a lot of context about the person. You’ve worked with them, you have some sense of their motivations, and you can hold them accountable afterwards. With an AI system, it’s much less clear how much reassurance you should get from its previous good behaviour. A system might behave well in all the situations where you test it, but behave differently when it has an opportunity to do something harmful.

Another difference is scale. You might have AI systems taking an enormous number of actions, so having a human carefully review every sensitive action could be prohibitively expensive. You’re going to want to use automated monitoring, potentially including other AI systems. And then you have to ask whether the monitor can actually recognise a problematic action, and whether the system taking the action can fool it.

But there are also advantages. With AI systems, you can potentially record everything they do, restrict their access very precisely, and require approval before particular actions go through. You can also test your review process by deliberately having a system try to get harmful actions past it.

So I’d put less emphasis on whether the AI seems trustworthy, and more emphasis on whether the overall process can catch a system that is actively trying to get away with something.

r001.rationale: The response discusses AI systems potentially trying to evade monitoring, but does not compare how correlated scheming is across AI systems with espionage across human employees.
